newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ reverses NZ bank bill rally with statement.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ reverses NZ bank bill rally with statement.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 92.89 (PREV 92.97) 90-DAYS 7.49 (PREV 7.35)
OVERNIGHT CASH 7.55 PCT (PREV 7.75) US 5-YR 6.14 (PREV 6.15)
RBNZ MCI NZ/MCI 760.42 (PREV 761.62) Reuters NZ MCI -65 vs -63
By Simon Louisson
New Zealand bank bill rates closed 20 basis points above their intraday lows on Friday after the Reserve Bank issued its second warning in eight days that conditions were too loose.
Volumes were heavy in the bill market, with the September futures rallying to 93.02 as March quarter current account data came out much worse than predicted.
That precipitated a selloff in the kiwi dollar which in turn saw the Monetary Conditions Index fell to 748.57, more than 75 points below the Reserve Bank's stated desired level or 825.
And that prompted bank governor Don Brash to issue a statement saying conditions were too loose and the bank had not changed its 50 basis point comfort zone around 825.
Bills and futures sold off, somewhat reluctantly, with the September bills closing at 92.89 on volume of 7215.
Traders said they were unconvinced by Brash's statement.
Much of the tightening in the MCI came via the currency and local traders in both the currency and bill market sold into the rally.

"It was pretty much shrugged off. Everyone knows the CPI on Tuesday and the employment numbers next week are going to be the key," said one dealer. "What's the Reserve Bank going to do at this stage?"
"People are getting short at the extreme MCI levels and as soon as they do see the Reserve Bank they see it as an opportunity to sell their position back out again."
The MCI ended at 760, still 15 basis points outside the bank's comfort zone.
The bond market was more subdued with long bonds little changed from Thursday's levels.
Dealers were not impressed by the Reserve Bank's "jawboning".
"If that's the best they can to try and jawbone conditions back to where they would like them, I think they are going to have a nasty shock at some point soon," said one.
"I think the market might just take it to them and say 'If you guys think that conditions really should be tighter you have to do more about than just talk to us'."
"It could almost come back as 'we dare you to tighten in this economic environment. How much do you trust your economic model?'"
He said the statement did have some effect but he thinks it will be very short term. A flat CPI result on Tuesday would see the bank tested all over again.
Stuart Marshall, economist with Bancorp said the $4.5 billion March year current account deficit was miles away from expectations.
"When the American and European markets awake to this data, the currency could come under further pressure," he said.

"The deficit was forecast by most analysts to deteriorate further and move out to 5.0 percent of GDP but today's figure cause us some concern that this happening rather too quickly and therefore (will) upset offshore investors."
-- Simon Louisson, Wellington newsroom, 64 4 4734 746
